title: HTTP Client Fundamentals
description: Making requests with Angular's HttpClient and understanding its observable-based, cold-request model.

blocks.title: Cold Observables, Not Promises
blocks.content: `HttpClient` methods return cold observables: no request is sent until something subscribes, and each new subscription triggers its own independent request. Response typing (`http.get<User>(url)`) tells the compiler the expected shape but performs no runtime validation of the actual JSON.
keyPoints: Subscribing twice to the same `http.get()` call issues two separate HTTP requests — use `shareReplay()` or a store to share one response.
`HttpClient` automatically parses JSON responses and surfaces non-2xx responses as an `HttpErrorResponse` through the error channel.
Type parameters are a compile-time convenience only — validate untrusted response shapes explicitly if correctness matters.

blocks.explanation: Nothing is sent over the network until a component subscribes (directly, via the `async` pipe, or via `toSignal()`).

blocks.question: A component binds the same `http.get()` observable to two different places in its template with two separate `async` pipes. What happens, and how do you fix it?
blocks.answer: Two subscriptions mean two separate HTTP requests fire for the same data. Fix it by sharing one subscription — pipe the observable through `shareReplay({ bufferSize: 1, refCount: true })` before binding it twice, or subscribe once (e.g. via `toSignal()`) and read the resulting signal in both template locations.
blocks.explanation: This is a common source of duplicate network calls in Angular apps, and it's exactly why `ContentService` in this app caches its `subjects$` observable with `shareReplay` rather than exposing the raw `http.get()` call.

For implementation, Separate transport DTOs from UI/domain models. Perform mapping in one place so backend naming or nullability changes do not leak across the application. Use interceptors only for cross-cutting behavior such as correlation IDs, authentication headers, common error envelopes, and telemetry. Do not hide feature-specific business rules in interceptors.

Finally, Add contract tests and log API version and correlation IDs for production diagnosis.

title: Route Guards
description: Controlling navigation with functional CanActivate/CanDeactivate guards — and their real security limits.

blocks.title: Functional Guards
blocks.content: Modern Angular guards are plain functions (`CanActivateFn`, `CanDeactivateFn`, etc.) registered on a route's `canActivate` array, run through `inject()` for dependencies. A guard returns `true`/`false`, a `UrlTree` (to redirect), or an observable/promise resolving to one of those.
keyPoints: Returning a `UrlTree` (e.g. `inject(Router).parseUrl('/login')`) is the idiomatic way to redirect from a guard instead of manually calling `router.navigate()` and returning `false`.
`CanDeactivate` guards protect against accidental navigation away from unsaved work (e.g. a dirty form).
Guards run on every matching navigation, including browser back/forward and programmatic navigation.

blocks.explanation: The guard is a pure function with dependencies pulled via `inject()` — no class or constructor boilerplate required.

blocks.question: Is a route guard a security boundary? Why or why not?
blocks.answer: No. A guard only controls client-side navigation inside the already-downloaded Angular application — it improves UX by hiding routes a user shouldn't casually reach, but the underlying JavaScript and any data the guarded component would fetch are still present in the bundle and reachable by directly calling the API. Every protected operation must be authorized again on the server.
blocks.explanation: This is one of the most common senior-level 'gotcha' questions: candidates who say a guard 'protects' a route usually haven't internalized that all client-side logic is inherently visible and bypassable.

title: Reactive Forms
description: Building typed, validated forms with FormGroup/FormControl and observing value/status changes.

blocks.title: An Explicit Model in TypeScript
blocks.content: Reactive forms define the entire form structure and validation rules in the component class as a typed `FormGroup` tree, rather than inferring structure from template directives. Strictly-typed forms (`FormGroup<{...}>`) catch mismatched control names and value types at compile time.
keyPoints: `valueChanges` and `statusChanges` are observables — pipe them through `debounceTime`, `distinctUntilChanged`, etc. for expensive validation or autosave.
Client-side validators (`Validators.required`, custom validator functions) improve UX; the server remains the authority on whether data is actually valid.
Reactive forms scale better than template-driven forms for dynamic, deeply nested, or heavily-tested forms.

blocks.explanation: `nonNullable: true` keeps the control's value type as `string` instead of `string | null`, and the debounced `valueChanges` stream avoids checking availability on every keystroke.

blocks.question: A save button should be disabled while the form is invalid or a save request is in flight, and should show a spinner during the save. How would you model this with reactive forms and signals?
blocks.answer: Convert `form.statusChanges` to a signal with `toSignal()` (or track validity via `form.valid` inside a `computed()` reading a signal that mirrors form state), add a local `saving = signal(false)` toggled around the save call, and bind the button's `disabled` to `computed(() => !formValid() || saving())`.
blocks.explanation: Keeping the 'is this safe to submit' logic as a single derived boolean (rather than checking `form.invalid` and a loading flag separately in the template) avoids subtly inconsistent UI states.

title: Application Architecture & Folder Structure
description: Organizing a growing Angular app around feature boundaries instead of technical layers.

blocks.title: Core, Shared, Features
blocks.content: A common, scalable structure splits an Angular app into `core/` (app-wide singletons: layout, auth, HTTP interceptors — imported once), `shared/` (stateless, reusable presentation components/pipes/directives with no business logic), and `features/` (one folder per business capability, each importing only from core/shared, never from another feature directly).
keyPoints: A feature should expose a small, intentional public surface (its routed components) — internals stay private to the feature folder.
`shared/` should never accumulate business logic; if a 'shared' component starts needing feature-specific state, it usually means it isn't actually shared.
Lint rules (e.g. module/import boundaries) can enforce these dependency directions automatically so architecture doesn't erode as the app and team grow.

blocks.code:
src/app/
  core/        (layout, auth, http interceptors — provided once)
  shared/      (dumb, reusable UI: buttons, cards, pipes)
  features/
    dashboard/
    subjects/
    practice/    (imports core + shared only, never another feature)
blocks.explanation: This is exactly the structure this app uses (`core/`, `shared/`, `features/*`) — each feature folder is self-contained and only reaches into `core`/`shared`.

blocks.question: Two features need to show the same 'topic card' UI. Where does that component belong, and where does the data for it come from?
blocks.answer: The presentational card component (markup/styling only, driven entirely by `@Input()`s) belongs in `shared/components`. The data it displays should come from a `core/services` data-access service (or a feature-owned store, if the data is feature-specific) — never duplicated inside each feature — so both features read from the same source of truth.
blocks.explanation: This distinction — shared presentation vs. centralized data ownership — is exactly why this app's `TopicCardComponent` lives in `shared/components` while all progress/bookmark state lives in single `core/services` stores that every feature reads from.

title: Handling one million backend records
description: Senior/lead scenario: An API can return 1,000,000 transaction records. The business asks you to display them in an Angular data grid with filtering, sorting, selection, and export. How would you design the UI?

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
Think of the grid as a window into a very large data set, not as the owner of that data. The server owns filtering, sorting, aggregation, and export because it has the full data and can do the work without blocking the browser.

The Angular app owns interaction: query state, cancellation, rendering visible rows, selection state, and clear feedback. Good performance comes from reducing data movement and DOM work before trying to optimize templates.

Selection and export also need separate models. Selection should be based on ids or a query-based all-matching model, and export should be a backend workflow using the query snapshot.
keyPoints: Do not download or render the entire dataset. Make pagination, filtering, sorting, and aggregation server-driven, and return only the columns and page required by the current view.

Use cursor-based pagination for frequently changing datasets; use offset pagination only when stable page numbers are a hard requirement. Keep the query state in the URL so the view is shareable and restorable.
Render only visible rows using virtual scrolling. Use trackBy, immutable row models, OnPush or signal-based rendering, and avoid expensive functions or pipes in every cell.
Cancel stale requests with switchMap or AbortSignal, debounce free-text filters, cache recent queries with an expiry, and prefetch the next page only when network and memory budgets allow it.
Run exports as an asynchronous backend job. The UI should submit the filters, display progress, and download the generated file rather than building a million-row file in the browser.
Measure response size, scripting time, heap growth, long tasks, scroll FPS, and Core Web Vitals before choosing a final page size.

blocks.question: An API can return 1,000,000 transaction records. The business asks you to display them in an Angular data grid with filtering, sorting, selection, and export. How would you design the UI?
blocks.answer:
I would not treat one million transactions as a browser data set. The grid should be a query screen over server data, so the browser only receives the current page, visible columns, and summary values it actually needs.

The query state would include filters, sort, page size, selected columns, and a cursor. I would keep that state in the URL so the view can be shared or restored. For changing transaction data, cursor paging is usually safer than offset paging because new rows can appear while the user is browsing.

In Angular, I would render only visible rows with virtual scrolling, stable row ids, trackBy, and cheap cell templates. The component should use OnPush or signals and avoid doing work in every cell on every change detection pass.

Requests need to be cancellable. A debounced filter stream with distinctUntilChanged and switchMap, or AbortSignal, prevents an old response from replacing a newer result. Recent queries can be cached briefly, but only with clear memory and freshness limits.

Export is not a grid feature running in the browser. The UI should submit the same filters to a backend export job, show progress, and download the generated file when it is ready.

I would prove the design with payload size, API latency, scripting time, heap growth, scroll FPS, long tasks, cancellation behavior, and accessibility checks on a normal user machine.

title: Choosing micro-frontends
description: Senior/lead scenario: Five business units want independent deployment of their Angular applications inside one portal. Would you choose micro-frontends?

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
Micro-frontends are mainly an ownership and deployment tool. The technical question is how much independence the teams really need and how much runtime complexity the product can afford.

A good design keeps the shell stable and boring, makes remote contracts explicit, and avoids hidden coupling through shared services or global state. Failure isolation, versioning, security, and observability matter as much as loading the remote code.

The decision should be tested against alternatives, because many teams only need modular boundaries and release discipline, not full runtime composition.
keyPoints: Start with the organizational problem. Micro-frontends are justified when teams need genuine release autonomy, separate ownership, and bounded business domains; they are not a default performance solution.
Define shell responsibilities: authentication, navigation, global error handling, feature discovery, design tokens, and cross-application telemetry.
Keep integration contracts small and versioned. Prefer URL, custom events, or typed platform APIs over sharing mutable services across remotes.
Control framework duplication and incompatible shared dependencies. Decide whether Angular is singleton-shared or isolated, and test failure when a remote is unavailable.
Establish design-system governance, accessibility standards, release compatibility, local development, observability correlation, and security review.
Compare alternatives such as a modular monolith, route-owned deployables, or backend-for-frontend separation. Choose the simplest architecture that meets autonomy needs.

blocks.question: Five business units want independent deployment of their Angular applications inside one portal. Would you choose micro-frontends?
blocks.answer:
I would start with the reason the teams want micro-frontends. They make sense when separate business units need real ownership and release independence for bounded parts of the product. I would not choose them just because the app is large or because they sound modern.

The shell should have a small, clear job: authentication handoff, navigation, layout, global errors, feature discovery, design tokens, and telemetry. Business behavior should live inside the remote applications, not in a tangled shared layer.

The integration contract has to stay small and versioned. I prefer routes, URLs, custom events, or typed platform APIs over sharing mutable Angular services across applications. Shared state between remotes is where many micro-frontend systems become hard to change.

I would decide how Angular and dependencies are shared. Singleton sharing can reduce bundle size but creates version coupling. Isolation costs more JavaScript but gives teams more freedom.

Operationally, I would require design-system rules, accessibility standards, compatible release testing, local development support, correlated observability, and a way for the shell to survive a broken remote.

Before committing, I would compare this with a modular monolith or separately owned routes in one Angular workspace. The simplest design that gives the teams the autonomy they need is usually the best answer.

Telemetry should include the shell version, remote version, and failure reason so the team can disable or roll back the bad remote quickly.

title: Selecting state management
description: Senior/lead scenario: A team proposes NgRx for every component. Another team wants only signals and services. How do you decide?

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
State management is about scope, lifetime, ownership, and coordination. The right tool depends on who reads the state, who changes it, how long it lives, and how risky inconsistent updates are.

Signals are great for simple local reactivity and clear derived values. NgRx is stronger when changes are event-like, cross-feature, asynchronous, and need a traceable history.

The goal is not fewer libraries or more libraries. The goal is predictable state changes with the least complexity that still protects the product.
keyPoints: Classify state first: local UI state, route state, server cache, cross-feature workflow state, and durable user preferences have different needs.
Keep local state close to the component using signals or component stores. Treat server state as a cache with loading, error, freshness, cancellation, and invalidation semantics.
Use a global event-driven store when many features coordinate around complex workflows, auditability, undo, time-travel debugging, or predictable effects.

Evaluate boilerplate, team skill, testability, debugging tools, persistence, concurrency, and ownership. A small app can be damaged by over-engineering; a complex app can be damaged by ad hoc shared services.
Expose read-only selectors and explicit commands. Avoid components mutating shared objects directly.
Document the decision and define thresholds for introducing a stronger state solution later.

blocks.question: A team proposes NgRx for every component. Another team wants only signals and services. How do you decide?
blocks.answer:
I would not choose NgRx or signals as a rule for every component. I would first classify the state: local UI state, route state, server cache, cross-feature workflow state, and user preferences all have different needs.

Local state should stay close to where it is used. Signals, component state, or a small component store are usually enough for expanded panels, form draft values, selected tabs, and view-only calculations.

Server state should be treated as a cache, not as random shared variables. It needs loading, error, freshness, cancellation, invalidation, and sometimes optimistic update behavior.

A global event-driven store is useful when many features coordinate around the same workflow or when the team needs predictable effects, auditability, undo, replay, or strong debugging tools. That is where NgRx can earn its boilerplate.

Whatever we choose, components should read through selectors or readonly signals and change state through explicit commands. Directly mutating shared objects is how small shortcuts become production bugs.

I would document the decision and the threshold for moving to a stronger model later, so the architecture can grow without making every component pay the cost on day one.

title: Dynamic forms driven by metadata
description: Senior/lead scenario: A product team wants a form engine where the backend controls fields, validation, visibility, and layout. How would you design it?

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
A metadata form works when the schema is a contract, not a programming language. The backend describes allowed form structure, and the Angular app renders it through a small set of trusted components.

The hard part is not creating text boxes dynamically. The hard part is versioning, validation ownership, safe conditional logic, saved draft migration, accessibility, and observability when a bad schema ships.

Keep the engine boring and explicit. Each new field type or rule should be a product decision with tests, not a loophole for unlimited behavior.
keyPoints: Define a versioned schema rather than sending executable expressions. Include field type, stable key, label token, validation rules, permissions, default value, and layout hints.
Map schema types to a controlled registry of Angular components. Unknown types must fail safely and be observable.
Create a recursive form model with typed adapters where practical. Keep business validation authoritative on the server and mirror user-friendly checks on the client.
Represent conditional visibility and dependencies as a safe declarative rule language. Detect dependency cycles and avoid evaluating arbitrary JavaScript.
Support accessibility, localization, draft persistence, analytics, and migration of saved forms when schema versions change.
Cache schemas with version/ETag and test representative configurations, not only individual field components.

blocks.question: A product team wants a form engine where the backend controls fields, validation, visibility, and layout. How would you design it?
blocks.answer:
I would design this as a controlled form platform, not as a backend sending Angular code. The backend should send a versioned schema with field type, stable key, label token, validators, permissions, defaults, and layout hints.

Angular would map each supported field type to a known component registry. If the schema asks for an unknown type, the form should fail safely, log it clearly, and avoid rendering something half broken.

The form model can be recursive for groups, arrays, and nested sections. I would use typed adapters where practical, but the server remains authoritative for business validation because client checks are mainly for fast feedback.

Conditional visibility should use a small declarative rule language, not arbitrary JavaScript. The engine should detect dependency cycles and keep rule evaluation predictable.

Production details matter here: accessibility, localization, drafts, analytics, permissions, and migration of saved answers when schema versions change. Schema caching with ETags or versions helps avoid repeated downloads without hiding updates.

I would test real form configurations, not only individual field components, because most failures happen when validation, visibility, layout, and permissions interact.

title: Centralized error handling
description: Senior/lead scenario: The application shows generic popups for every error and production logs lack context. Design a better error strategy.

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
Good error handling separates expected product outcomes from unexpected defects. A validation error, an expired session, and a null pointer are different problems and need different UX, telemetry, and ownership.

The API layer should turn transport details into meaningful application outcomes. Components then show helpful recovery instead of spreading status-code logic across the UI.

Centralization is useful for consistency and telemetry, but it should not remove local context. The strongest design combines local handling for known states with global capture for what escaped.
keyPoints: Define an error taxonomy: validation, authentication, authorization, conflict, rate limit, timeout, connectivity, dependency failure, and unexpected defect.
Translate transport errors into domain errors near the API boundary. Components should react to meaningful outcomes rather than HTTP status numbers.
Use a global handler for truly unhandled errors and framework failures, not for swallowing expected business errors.
Show actionable, localized messages with recovery options. Preserve user input and avoid exposing stack traces or sensitive server details.
Attach correlation ID, route, feature, app version, user-safe identifiers, and recent action context to telemetry. Redact PII and tokens.
Add error-rate alerts and track whether users recover or abandon the flow.

blocks.question: The application shows generic popups for every error and production logs lack context. Design a better error strategy.
blocks.answer:
I would stop treating every failure as the same popup. The first step is an error taxonomy: validation, authentication, authorization, conflict, rate limit, timeout, connectivity, dependency failure, and unexpected defects.

HTTP errors should be translated near the API boundary into domain errors the rest of the app understands. A component should not need to know whether a conflict was status 409 or a custom backend code; it should know the user can reload, edit, retry, or contact support.

The global Angular error handler is for unhandled errors, framework failures, and last-resort telemetry. It should not swallow expected business errors that the feature can handle better.

User messages should be specific, localizable, and safe. They should preserve user input, offer a recovery path, and never expose stack traces, internal ids, tokens, or sensitive server details.

Telemetry needs context: correlation id, route, feature, app version, safe user or tenant identifiers, and the action that failed. It also needs redaction so the error system does not become a PII leak.

I would add alerts around user impact, such as checkout failures or repeated save errors, and track whether users recover or abandon the flow.

blocks.question: Which errors should be retried automatically, and which should be shown immediately?
blocks.answer: I would automatically retry transient failures such as network drops, timeouts, 429s, and some 5xx responses, only when the request is idempotent or has an idempotency key. Retries should use backoff, jitter, and a small limit. I would show validation errors, authorization failures, authentication problems, conflicts, and payment or mutation uncertainty immediately because retrying can confuse the user or repeat side effects.
blocks.explanation: It is strong because it connects retry behavior to error type, idempotency, and user trust.

title: Client-side caching strategy
description: Senior/lead scenario: A reference-data API is called repeatedly across routes. The data changes a few times per day. How would you cache it?

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
A cache is a promise about freshness, ownership, and invalidation. Before adding shareReplay, decide who the response belongs to, how old it may be, and what event makes it wrong.

Reference data often fits a service-level cache because many routes need the same values. The danger is making that cache permanent or too broad, especially across users, tenants, locales, or permissions.

The best cache is observable in production. If you cannot tell hit rate, age, and invalidation behavior, it is hard to trust.
keyPoints: Define freshness and ownership first. Cache by complete query key and include user/tenant context where responses differ.
Use a service-level cache with shareReplay or signal state, but add expiry, invalidation, error reset, and a way to force refresh. Avoid an immortal observable that permanently caches a failure.
Use ETag or Last-Modified for conditional requests where supported. Prefer stale-while-revalidate when slightly stale data is acceptable.
Invalidate after mutations or version changes. Do not cache sensitive responses in persistent browser storage unless explicitly approved.
Bound memory with an LRU or maximum-entry policy for parameterized queries.
Expose cache status so diagnostics can distinguish network calls from cache hits.

blocks.question: A reference-data API is called repeatedly across routes. The data changes a few times per day. How would you cache it?
blocks.answer:
I would first define what fresh means for this reference data. If it changes a few times per day, users can probably tolerate slightly stale data, but we still need clear expiry and invalidation rules.

The cache key must include the full query and any user, tenant, locale, or permission context that changes the response. A shared reference-data cache that ignores tenant is a security bug, not an optimization.

In Angular, I would put the cache in a service using shareReplay or signal state, but not as an immortal observable. It needs TTL, forced refresh, invalidation after relevant mutations, and reset behavior after errors.

If the API supports ETag or Last-Modified, I would use conditional requests. Stale-while-revalidate is a good fit when showing the last known value quickly is acceptable while a background refresh updates the cache.

For parameterized queries, I would bound memory with an LRU or max-entry policy. Persistent browser storage should be avoided for sensitive responses unless there is explicit approval.

Diagnostics should show cache hits, misses, refreshes, and failures so the team can tell whether performance improved or whether the cache is hiding stale data.

blocks.question: How would you prevent cache leakage between two logged-in users on a shared device?

On logout, account switch, token refresh that changes identity, or tenant change, I would clear in-memory caches and avoid reusing persistent entries unless they are encrypted, approved, and keyed safely. I would also make the cache service live inside the authenticated app scope rather than a process-wide singleton when possible.
blocks.explanation: It is strong because it treats cache isolation as part of the security model, not just a cleanup detail.

title: Real-time dashboard architecture
description: Senior/lead scenario: A risk dashboard receives thousands of updates per second over WebSocket. How would you keep the Angular UI responsive?

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
Real-time UI design is about turning an event firehose into a useful state view. The browser is not a message archive, and the DOM should not be the unit of streaming.

The important ideas are aggregation, normalization, throttled rendering, and explicit freshness. Users need correct and timely decisions, not a repaint for every packet.

Reliability is part of the design. A dashboard must know when it missed data, recovered from replay, or needs a fresh snapshot.
keyPoints: Do not render every event. Aggregate, sample, buffer, or window updates based on what the user can perceive and what the business requires.
Normalize data by entity ID and update only changed entities. Use signals/selectors with stable references and virtualize large lists.
Move expensive parsing or aggregation to a Web Worker when it consumes meaningful main-thread time.
Apply backpressure or server-side subscription filters. Define behavior for reconnect, replay, sequence gaps, duplicates, and stale data.
Pause or reduce updates for hidden tabs and off-screen widgets. Mark freshness and last-update time clearly.
Measure dropped frames, long tasks, message lag, heap growth, and reconnection rates.

blocks.question: A risk dashboard receives thousands of updates per second over WebSocket. How would you keep the Angular UI responsive?
blocks.answer:
I would not try to render thousands of WebSocket messages per second one by one. The UI should show the latest useful state at a rate humans can read, not every raw event.

The stream should be normalized by entity id. Incoming events update a data model, and Angular only receives changed view models with stable references. Large lists should be virtualized and rendered with OnPush or signals.

If parsing, aggregation, or risk calculations take real main-thread time, I would move that work to a Web Worker. The main thread should stay focused on input, layout, and paint.

Backpressure matters. I would use server-side filters or subscriptions so the client only receives the instruments, accounts, or risk groups the user is viewing. The system also needs rules for reconnect, replay, duplicate events, sequence gaps, and stale data.

Hidden tabs and off-screen widgets should pause or reduce update frequency. The UI should clearly show freshness and last update time so users know when data is delayed.

I would measure dropped frames, long tasks, message lag, heap growth, reconnect rates, and sequence recovery, then tune the update window and subscription model with real traffic.

Duplicate or out-of-order events should be ignored based on sequence and entity version.

title: Using @defer correctly
description: Senior/lead scenario: A product page contains reviews, recommendations, and an AI assistant below the fold. How would you use Angular deferrable views?

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
Deferrable views are a way to move JavaScript and rendering work away from the critical path. They help when the user can get value from the page before that code exists.

The mistake is thinking deferred always means better. If the user immediately needs the content, deferral turns one load into two waits and can make the page feel slower.

Use @defer with a product reason, a trigger, a fallback state, and measurement. Bundle size alone is not the full user experience.
keyPoints: Defer non-critical content using triggers such as viewport, interaction, idle, or timer based on user value and dependency cost.
Provide meaningful placeholder, loading, and error states with stable dimensions to avoid layout shift.
Ensure deferred dependencies satisfy Angular requirements and are not referenced elsewhere in the same file in a way that makes them eager.
Do not defer content required for initial user task, accessibility, or search visibility without understanding SSR and hydration behavior.
Prefetch only when network and device conditions allow. Measure whether the deferred chunk is actually excluded from initial load.
Test keyboard users and screen readers so interaction-triggered content remains discoverable.

blocks.question: A product page contains reviews, recommendations, and an AI assistant below the fold. How would you use Angular deferrable views?
blocks.answer:
@defer is useful for content that is not needed for the first task on the page. On a product page, reviews, recommendations, and an AI assistant below the fold are good candidates if the main product content and buy flow stay immediately usable.

I would choose triggers based on value and cost. Reviews might defer on viewport, recommendations might prefetch on idle, and the AI assistant might load on interaction because it is expensive and not every user opens it.

The deferred area still needs good UX. Placeholders should have stable dimensions to avoid layout shift, loading states should be meaningful, and errors should give the user a way to retry or continue.

I would check the Angular constraints carefully. A component meant to be deferred should not also be imported or referenced in the same file in a way that pulls it into the eager bundle.

Search, accessibility, and SSR matter. I would not defer content that is important for SEO, screen-reader discovery, or the first user task unless the rendering and hydration behavior is understood.

Finally, I would verify with a production build that the chunk is actually split, initial JavaScript went down, layout stayed stable, and keyboard and screen-reader users can still discover the deferred content.

blocks.answer: @defer can reduce initial JavaScript but hurt UX when the deferred content is likely to be needed immediately, such as reviews visible on common mobile viewports or an assistant opened during the main task. It can also hurt if the placeholder shifts layout, the trigger is hard for keyboard users to reach, or the network is slow and the second chunk loads at the worst moment.
blocks.explanation: It is strong because it balances bundle cost with timing, layout stability, and accessibility.

title: SSR, hydration, and rendering strategy
description: Senior/lead scenario: A public Angular site needs fast first content and SEO, while the authenticated dashboard is highly interactive. What rendering strategy would you use?

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
Rendering strategy is a route-level decision. Public, stable, search-sensitive content benefits from prerendering or SSR, while private interactive screens often gain less from server rendering.

Hydration is a contract that the HTML produced on the server is the same HTML Angular expects in the browser. Any environment-dependent value can break that contract.

Performance must include both first paint and readiness to interact. SSR that paints fast but hydrates slowly may still feel bad.
keyPoints: Choose rendering per route: prerender stable marketing pages, SSR dynamic public pages, and client rendering for private areas where SEO is irrelevant.
Use hydration so the client reuses server-rendered DOM. Prevent server/client output mismatch caused by random values, dates, direct browser APIs, or different data.
Transfer data already fetched on the server to avoid duplicate client requests and visible flicker.
Use incremental hydration or deferred islands for expensive below-the-fold interactions.
Keep authentication and personalized caching safe; never cache one user response for another.
Measure server latency, first content, hydration cost, interaction readiness, and error rates.

blocks.question: A public Angular site needs fast first content and SEO, while the authenticated dashboard is highly interactive. What rendering strategy would you use?
blocks.answer:
I would choose rendering per route, not one strategy for the whole Angular app. Stable marketing pages can be prerendered, dynamic public pages can use SSR, and the authenticated dashboard can mostly be client-rendered if SEO is irrelevant.

For public pages, SSR helps first content and search visibility. Hydration should let Angular reuse the server-rendered DOM instead of throwing it away and rebuilding it.

The hard part is making server and client output match. Random ids, Date.now, locale differences, direct browser APIs, and data fetched differently on each side can all create hydration problems.

Data fetched on the server should be transferred to the client so Angular does not immediately refetch and flicker. Expensive below-the-fold interaction can use deferred views or incremental hydration where appropriate.

Personalized and authenticated content needs careful caching. The server must never cache one user's dashboard response and serve it to another user.

I would measure server response time, first content, hydration cost, interaction readiness, duplicate requests, and hydration error rates by route.

Then I would force deterministic formatting by using an explicit locale and timezone, usually UTC or the business timezone, instead of relying on the server or browser default. I would reproduce the issue with tests that run under the failing TZ setting and check that server-fetched data is transferred rather than recalculated differently on the client.
blocks.explanation: It is strong because it focuses on deterministic rendering across environments, which is the usual cause of timezone-only hydration bugs.

title: Component API design
description: Senior/lead scenario: A shared table component has 70 inputs and emits low-level events. How would you redesign it?

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
Component API design is about choosing the right extension points. Inputs are good for simple values, but too many inputs create combinations no one understands or tests.

A shared component should expose stable concepts and hide internal mechanics. Consumers should be able to customize allowed areas without depending on private markup or event details.

The design is only successful if it can evolve. Documentation, accessible defaults, and contract tests are part of the API.
keyPoints: Start from supported use cases and separate core table behavior from optional features. A component should have a coherent responsibility.
Prefer a small typed configuration object for related stable options, but do not hide every behavior in one untyped mega-object.
Expose domain-neutral events such as queryChange, selectionChange, and actionRequest. Avoid emitting raw DOM events or internal implementation details.
Use content projection, directives, and templates for extensibility instead of adding an input for every custom cell.
Provide accessible defaults, deterministic keyboard behavior, and a migration/deprecation policy.
Document performance expectations and use harnesses or contract tests so consumers are protected during refactoring.

blocks.question: A shared table component has 70 inputs and emits low-level events. How would you redesign it?
blocks.answer:
A table with 70 inputs is usually trying to be too many products at once. I would start by listing the supported use cases and separating core table behavior from optional features.

The public API should describe what consumers need, not how the table happens to work internally. Related stable options can live in small typed configuration objects, but I would avoid one giant untyped config bag that hides every behavior.

Events should be domain-neutral and meaningful, such as queryChange, selectionChange, rowAction, or actionRequest. Emitting raw DOM events or internal state leaks implementation details and makes refactoring painful.

For extension, I would use content projection, directives, and typed templates for custom cells, row actions, and empty states. That is cleaner than adding a boolean input for every consumer request.

Accessibility and keyboard behavior should be part of the component contract. Shared components also need documentation, examples, migration notes, and a deprecation policy.

I would protect consumers with harnesses or contract tests, so the table can be refactored without silently breaking every feature that uses it.

For example, a custom cell template, row action menu, or empty state should be projected or provided as a template rather than controlled by another boolean. Booleans are fine for small stable options, but they break down when combinations multiply.

title: Dynamic component and plugin architecture
description: Senior/lead scenario: Customers can enable optional dashboard widgets delivered by different teams. Design a safe plugin model.

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
A plugin model is a contract between a platform and independently delivered features. The host must define what plugins may do, how they are loaded, how they clean up, and how they fail.

Dynamic component loading by itself is not the architecture. Security, versioning, permissions, observability, and resource limits decide whether the system stays safe.

Trust level drives isolation. Internal plugins can often share more runtime, while third-party plugins need a much smaller and more defensive boundary.
keyPoints: Define a versioned plugin manifest containing ID, compatible platform version, permissions, route/widget registrations, and asset locations.
Expose a narrow platform SDK for data access, events, navigation, and telemetry. Plugins should not import host internals.
Load plugins lazily and isolate failures. Validate manifests, verify origin and integrity, and enforce a security review before registration.
Define lifecycle hooks, cleanup, state persistence, accessibility requirements, and resource budgets.
Use dependency injection tokens or typed registries for in-process plugins; use stronger isolation such as iframes when code is less trusted.
Support compatibility testing and the ability to disable a faulty plugin remotely.

blocks.question: Customers can enable optional dashboard widgets delivered by different teams. Design a safe plugin model.
blocks.answer:
I would start with a plugin manifest. Each plugin should declare its id, compatible platform version, permissions, widget or route registrations, asset locations, and any required feature flags.

The host should expose a narrow platform SDK for data access, navigation, events, and telemetry. Plugins should not import random host internals or reach into shared state directly.

Loading should be lazy and failure-safe. The host validates the manifest, checks origin and integrity, loads the plugin only when needed, and shows a contained fallback if it fails.

Lifecycle is important. Plugins need clear mount, update, destroy, cleanup, persistence, accessibility, and resource-budget rules so they do not leak subscriptions or slow the dashboard.

For trusted internal plugins, Angular DI tokens or typed registries may be enough. For less trusted code, I would use stronger isolation such as sandboxed iframes and message-based communication.

The platform should support compatibility tests and a remote disable switch. A bad plugin should be removable without redeploying the whole portal.

title: Internationalization at scale
description: Senior/lead scenario: The application supports 20 locales, plural rules, currencies, time zones, and right-to-left languages. What architecture would you use?

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
Internationalization is data modeling, formatting, layout, and release process. Translation files are only one piece.

The key mental model is to keep canonical business data stable and localize only the presentation. A localized label should never become a program value.

Scale comes from automation and design-system support: pseudo-locales, RTL, plural rules, long text, currency formats, and timezone behavior must be tested continuously.
keyPoints: Use message IDs and locale-aware formatting, not string concatenation. Keep business values separate from presentation formatting.
Decide whether translations are compile-time or runtime loaded based on deployment and content-update needs. Lazy load locale bundles by route or language.
Store timestamps in an unambiguous format and convert using the user or business timezone. Define rules for date-only values separately.
Support RTL at the design-system level using logical CSS properties and mirrored directional icons where appropriate.
Automate missing-key checks, pseudo-localization, overflow testing, and translation review.
Never use localized display strings as IDs, cache keys, or values sent back to APIs.

blocks.question: The application supports 20 locales, plural rules, currencies, time zones, and right-to-left languages. What architecture would you use?
blocks.answer:
I would build internationalization into the platform, not treat it as text replacement at the end. Messages should use stable ids and locale-aware formatting, not string concatenation.

Business values should stay separate from display text. Dates, currencies, numbers, and plural rules should be formatted at the edge for the user's locale or the business-required locale.

The team needs to decide whether translations are compiled into builds or loaded at runtime. Runtime loading helps if content changes often or languages are enabled independently; compile-time can be simpler for static releases.

Time zones need explicit rules. Store instants in an unambiguous format, define how date-only values work, and convert using the user timezone or business timezone depending on the domain.

RTL cannot be a one-off page fix. The design system should use logical CSS properties, layout patterns that mirror correctly, and directional icons where needed.

I would automate missing-key checks, pseudo-localization, overflow testing, translation review, and tests that prove localized display strings are never used as ids, cache keys, or API values.

When displaying or grouping that transaction, I would format it using the market timezone, not the user's browser timezone. Date-only market values need their own rule so daylight saving changes do not shift the date accidentally.

title: Accessibility in Angular components
description: Senior/lead scenario: A custom dropdown looks correct but cannot be operated reliably with keyboard or screen reader. How would you fix it?

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
Accessibility is not a layer of ARIA sprinkled on top. A component is accessible when its semantics, focus behavior, keyboard model, visible state, and announcements all match what users expect.

Native controls are valuable because the platform already solved many of these details. Custom controls are possible, but they take discipline and testing.

For Angular teams, the best accessibility work often happens in shared components, where one correct implementation protects many screens.
keyPoints: Prefer a native select when it satisfies the requirement. Native elements provide semantics, focus behavior, and platform accessibility for free.
For a custom pattern, follow the appropriate WAI-ARIA interaction model: roles, relationships, active option, expanded state, and keyboard behavior must agree.
Manage focus predictably, support Escape and arrow keys, preserve visible focus, and do not trap focus unintentionally.
Announce asynchronous loading and errors without excessive live-region noise.
Test with keyboard only, automated tools, and at least one screen reader/browser combination. Include high zoom and high-contrast checks.
Put the behavior in the shared design system so every feature does not reimplement it.

blocks.question: A custom dropdown looks correct but cannot be operated reliably with keyboard or screen reader. How would you fix it?
blocks.answer:
I would first ask whether this really needs to be custom. If a native select satisfies the requirement, it gives semantics, focus behavior, keyboard support, and platform accessibility with much less risk.

If it must be custom, I would implement the correct WAI-ARIA pattern for the widget. Roles, labels, expanded state, active option, listbox relationship, and selected state all need to agree with the keyboard behavior.

Focus handling should be predictable. The user should be able to open it, move through options, select, dismiss with Escape, tab away, and always see where focus is.

Async loading and errors need accessible feedback without noisy announcements. A live region can help, but it should not repeat every small state change.

I would test it with keyboard only, automated accessibility tools, high zoom, high contrast, and at least one real screen reader and browser combination.

Once fixed, the behavior belongs in the shared design system. Every feature team should not rebuild a dropdown from scratch.

blocks.question: Why is adding role="button" to a div not enough?
blocks.answer: A div with role button only changes part of the semantic announcement. It still needs to be focusable, respond to Enter and Space like a real button, expose an accessible name and state, preserve visible focus, and work with assistive technology. In most cases, using a real button is simpler and more reliable.

title: Angular security and sanitization
description: Senior/lead scenario: A feature displays rich HTML received from a CMS. A developer proposes bypassSecurityTrustHtml. What is your response?

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
Angular security depends on context. Text interpolation, URL bindings, style bindings, and innerHTML have different risks, so the framework applies different protections.

Escaping, sanitizing, and trusting are not the same thing. A senior answer should make clear that trusting content is a security decision, not a cleaning step.

The safest pattern is a trusted content pipeline with a narrow rendering adapter, plus browser-level defenses like CSP and Trusted Types.
keyPoints: Treat CMS content as untrusted unless a documented trusted pipeline proves otherwise. Angular sanitization is a defense that should not be bypassed casually.
Sanitize on the server using an allowlist appropriate to the content model, and validate again at the rendering boundary where necessary.
Avoid direct DOM APIs and innerHTML for arbitrary values. Bind text as text and URLs through validated schemes and destinations.
Use bypass APIs only after a focused security review and keep them behind a small, audited wrapper with clear trusted-source types.
Add Content Security Policy and Trusted Types where feasible to reduce the impact of injection mistakes.
Test payloads involving scripts, event attributes, javascript URLs, SVG, style injection, and malformed markup.

blocks.question: A feature displays rich HTML received from a CMS. A developer proposes bypassSecurityTrustHtml. What is your response?
blocks.answer:
I would push back on using bypassSecurityTrustHtml as a quick fix. CMS content should be treated as untrusted unless there is a documented trusted publishing and sanitization pipeline.

Angular already escapes interpolation and sanitizes certain binding contexts. The bypass API is different: it tells Angular to stop protecting that value because the developer promises it is safe.

If rich HTML is required, I would define an allowlisted content model and sanitize on the server. At the Angular boundary, I would keep any trust conversion inside a small audited wrapper, not scattered across components.

I would also validate URLs, image sources, SVG, style attributes, and malformed markup. XSS payloads often hide in places that look like harmless content.

CSP and Trusted Types can reduce the damage of a missed injection bug. They do not replace sanitization, but they are good defense in depth.

Finally, I would test with malicious CMS payloads and review logs, telemetry, and previews to make sure unsafe HTML or PII is not leaking through another path.

blocks.question: What is the difference between escaping, sanitizing, and trusting content?
blocks.answer: Escaping turns special characters into text so markup is displayed instead of executed. Sanitizing parses content and removes or changes unsafe parts while allowing approved markup. Trusting does not clean anything; it marks a value as already safe and tells Angular not to sanitize it.
blocks.explanation: It is strong because it clearly separates three security concepts that are often confused in Angular interviews.

title: Content Security Policy in an Angular app
description: Senior/lead scenario: A bank requires a strict Content Security Policy, but the application uses third-party analytics, inline styles, and dynamic scripts. How do you proceed?

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
CSP is a browser-enforced boundary that limits where code and resources can come from. It is most useful when it is specific, measured, and aligned with how the app actually loads resources.

A strict policy is usually a migration, not a one-line change. Inline scripts, dynamic loaders, analytics tools, styles, and frames all need to be understood and often replaced.

The point is not to silence violations. The point is to reduce the blast radius of injection mistakes while keeping the app working.
keyPoints: Inventory every script, style, font, image, frame, worker, and network origin. Remove unnecessary third-party code before writing policy exceptions.
Start with report-only, collect violations, and move toward nonce/hash-based script policies rather than unsafe-inline.
Load third-party code through approved wrappers and verify whether it supports CSP. Avoid runtime script construction and eval-like behavior.
Configure frame-ancestors, object-src, base-uri, connect-src, and form-action deliberately, not only script-src.
Correlate violation reports with application version and route while respecting privacy.
Treat CSP as defense in depth; continue output encoding, sanitization, secure dependencies, and server authorization.

blocks.question: A bank requires a strict Content Security Policy, but the application uses third-party analytics, inline styles, and dynamic scripts. How do you proceed?
blocks.answer:
I would start with an inventory, not with a policy header. We need to know every script, style, image, font, frame, worker, and API origin the app uses.

Then I would remove third-party code that is not worth the risk. A strict CSP becomes much easier when the application is not carrying old analytics snippets and dynamic script loaders.

The rollout should begin in report-only mode. We can collect violations by route and app version, then replace unsafe-inline with nonces or hashes and remove eval-like behavior where possible.

Third-party integrations should go through approved wrappers. If a vendor cannot support the bank's CSP requirements, that is a product and security decision, not something to hide with a broad exception.

The policy should cover more than script-src. frame-ancestors, object-src, base-uri, connect-src, form-action, img-src, style-src, and worker-src all matter.

I would keep reminding the team that CSP is defense in depth. We still need output encoding, sanitization, dependency hygiene, server authorization, and secure session handling.

title: Large file upload
description: Senior/lead scenario: Users upload multi-gigabyte files through an Angular application. What design would you use?

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
Large upload design is about reliability and trust boundaries. Angular coordinates the workflow, but storage, validation, scanning, and final availability belong on backend-controlled infrastructure.

The file is too large to treat as one request. Chunking makes retry and resume practical, while checksums and server state keep the upload honest.

The user experience should reflect real upload state. Clear progress and recovery matter as much as the happy path.
keyPoints: Upload directly to object storage using short-lived signed URLs when possible so application servers do not proxy the entire file.
Use chunked or resumable upload with checksums, retry per chunk, pause/resume, and persisted upload state.
Validate file type, size, and business metadata on both client and server. Never trust the filename or MIME type supplied by the browser.
Display honest progress based on bytes acknowledged, not an artificial timer. Support cancellation and cleanup of abandoned uploads.
Scan uploaded content asynchronously before making it available and isolate it from executable origins.
Limit concurrent chunks based on network conditions and monitor failure rates and memory use.

blocks.question: Users upload multi-gigabyte files through an Angular application. What design would you use?
blocks.answer:
I would avoid sending multi-gigabyte files through the Angular app server when possible. The browser should upload directly to object storage using short-lived signed URLs, while the application backend controls authorization and metadata.

The upload should be chunked and resumable. Each chunk needs retry, checksum validation, and a way to pause, resume, or cancel without starting the whole file again.

Client validation is useful for fast feedback, but it is not trust. File size, type, extension, MIME type, and business metadata must also be validated on the server because the browser can lie.

Progress should be based on bytes accepted or acknowledged, not a fake timer. Users need honest states: waiting for URL, uploading, paused, retrying, processing, failed, cancelled, and complete.

After upload, the file should be scanned asynchronously before it is made available. Uploaded content should be isolated from executable origins so a bad file cannot become a script delivery path.

I would limit concurrent chunks based on network conditions and watch memory use, upload failures, retry rates, and abandoned uploads.

I would validate with interrupted-network tests, browser restart resume tests, checksum failures, virus-scan states, large-file memory profiles, and abandoned-upload cleanup metrics.

blocks.question: How would you resume an upload after the user closes and reopens the browser?
blocks.answer: I would create an upload session id and persist safe resume state in IndexedDB or local storage, such as file fingerprint, chunk size, completed chunks, and expiration. When the user returns, the app asks the server which chunks were accepted, gets fresh signed URLs, verifies the same file is selected, and resumes missing chunks with checksums. If the upload session expired, the UI should explain that a new upload is required.
blocks.explanation: It is strong because it covers both client resume state and server truth, which are both needed after a browser restart.

title: Exporting large reports
description: Senior/lead scenario: A business user wants a PDF and Excel export of a very large filtered table. Should the Angular app generate them?

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
Large export is a backend workflow with a frontend control panel. The browser starts the job and shows state; it should not become the report engine.

The important idea is preserving intent. The export must reflect the filter, sort, permissions, locale, and data snapshot the user submitted, not whatever the table happens to show later.

Security and audit matter because exported files leave the application boundary and are easy to share.
keyPoints: Use client-side generation only for small, bounded exports where the browser can safely hold the data and rendering cost.
For large exports, submit an export job with the current filter/sort definition. Generate the file on the backend, store it securely, and notify the user when ready.
Include an immutable query snapshot, user/tenant authorization, locale, timezone, and audit metadata in the job.
Show queued, processing, completed, failed, and expired states. Allow cancellation where backend processing supports it.
Protect download URLs with short lifetime and authorization checks, and redact data according to export permissions.
Measure export duration, queue depth, failure reasons, and download size.

blocks.question: A business user wants a PDF and Excel export of a very large filtered table. Should the Angular app generate them?
blocks.answer:
I would only generate exports in the Angular app for small, bounded data sets. For a very large filtered table, the browser should not fetch everything and build Excel or PDF locally.

The UI should submit an export job to the backend using the current filter, sort, selected columns, locale, timezone, and export format. The backend can generate the file with the right memory limits, queueing, and audit controls.

The job needs an immutable query snapshot. It should include user and tenant authorization, export permissions, and enough metadata to explain later what was exported and why.

The Angular screen should show queued, processing, completed, failed, expired, and cancelled states. If the job is long-running, users should be able to leave the page and return to the export history.

Download links should be short-lived and authorization-checked. Sensitive columns may need redaction even if they are visible in the grid, depending on export policy.

I would measure export duration, queue depth, failure reasons, file size, cancellation, and download success, because export systems often fail under end-of-month production load.

title: Feature flags and controlled rollout
description: Senior/lead scenario: A new payment flow must be released gradually by country, user group, and application version. How do you implement it?

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
Feature flags are controlled decision points in a release system. They are not permissions, and they are not a replacement for backend enforcement.

A good flag has ownership, a lifecycle, and observability. Without those, the codebase fills with branches no one understands.

Rollout quality depends on stable targeting and fast feedback. The team must know exactly which users saw which behavior when errors happen.
keyPoints: Evaluate flags in a trusted service or signed configuration and return only the decisions required by the user context.
Give each flag an owner, purpose, default, expiry date, and cleanup task. Flags are temporary architecture, not permanent conditional clutter.
Hide navigation and code paths consistently, but keep backend authorization independent of the flag.
Support percentage rollout with stable bucketing so users do not switch variants on every session.
Record flag state in telemetry and error reports so incidents can be correlated with rollout groups.
Provide a kill switch and test both enabled and disabled states in CI.

blocks.question: A new payment flow must be released gradually by country, user group, and application version. How do you implement it?
blocks.answer:
I would evaluate the flag decisions in a trusted service or from signed configuration, not by letting the browser decide who should get a payment flow. The Angular app should receive only the decisions needed for the current user context.

Each flag needs an owner, purpose, default value, rollout rules, expiry date, and cleanup task. Flags are useful during change, but old flags become permanent conditional clutter if nobody removes them.

The UI should hide navigation and route paths consistently when the flow is off. The backend still needs independent authorization and validation, because a disabled button is not a security boundary.

For gradual rollout, I would use country, user group, application version, and stable percentage bucketing. Stable bucketing prevents a user from switching variants every time they sign in.

Telemetry and error reports should include the relevant flag decisions. If payment errors rise only for one rollout group, the team needs to see that quickly.

A kill switch is required for a payment flow. CI should test both enabled and disabled states, and production should have a safe way to turn the feature off without redeploying.

blocks.question: What is the difference between a release flag, experiment flag, and permission?
blocks.answer: A release flag controls whether new code is exposed during rollout and should usually be removed after launch. An experiment flag assigns users to variants so the team can measure behavior, and it needs stable assignment and analysis rules. A permission is an authorization or entitlement decision and must be enforced by the backend, not only by the Angular UI.
blocks.explanation: It is strong because it separates deployment control, product experimentation, and security authorization.

title: Observability for frontend systems
description: Senior/lead scenario: Production users report intermittent slowness, but server dashboards look healthy. What frontend observability would you add?

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
Think of frontend observability as the missing half of production truth. The server can be healthy while the browser is downloading too much JavaScript, blocking on long tasks, failing to load a CDN asset, or spending too long rendering after data arrives.

A good model separates the journey into client startup, navigation, request time, response handling, rendering, and user action. Each piece should have enough context to connect it to a user-impacting flow without exposing private data.

The strongest Angular answer also treats observability as a product and operations feature. It needs version tags, route tags, feature flag state, sampling, privacy review, dashboards, and alerts that point to the affected users rather than a pile of raw logs.
keyPoints: Collect real-user performance: navigation timing, Core Web Vitals, route transitions, API latency, long tasks, resource failures, and JavaScript errors.
Correlate client requests with backend traces using a correlation or trace ID. Include app version, route, feature, device class, and network class.
Instrument key business journeys with start, success, validation failure, technical failure, and abandonment events.
Sample intelligently and redact PII, tokens, form values, and sensitive URLs. Obtain required privacy approvals.
Create dashboards and alerts around user impact, not only raw error count.
Use session replay only under strict privacy controls and masking, especially in financial applications.

blocks.question: Production users report intermittent slowness, but server dashboards look healthy. What frontend observability would you add?
blocks.answer:
I would add real-user monitoring first, because intermittent frontend slowness often does not show up in server dashboards. I want timing from real browsers: route changes, Core Web Vitals, API calls, JavaScript errors, resource failures, and long tasks on the main thread.

Then I would make every important client request traceable. The Angular app should send or receive a correlation ID so I can connect a slow checkout screen to the backend trace, the app version, the route, the device class, and the network type.

For business flows, I would instrument the journey, not only technical events. A payment flow, for example, should have events for start, validation failure, backend failure, success, and abandonment. That tells me whether users are actually blocked.

I would be strict about privacy. Telemetry should sample intelligently and remove tokens, account numbers, form values, sensitive URLs, and other PII. Session replay can help, but only with masking, consent, and clear rules, especially in banking or healthcare.

Finally, I would build dashboards around user impact. Error count alone is not enough. I care which version, route, feature flag, browser, or region is hurting users, and I want alerts tied to failed journeys or slow real-user performance.

title: Testing strategy for a large Angular application
description: Senior/lead scenario: The project has thousands of brittle unit tests but still releases defects. How would you redesign the test strategy?

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
A healthy test strategy is shaped like risk, not like the component tree. Some code needs tiny pure tests, some needs rendering tests, some needs contracts, and some needs a real browser journey.

Brittle tests often know too much about how Angular components are built. They break when markup or private methods change, even though the user-visible behavior is the same. Better tests ask: what can the user do, what should they see, and what contract does this boundary promise?

Large applications also need feedback loops. When defects escape, the team should ask which layer should have caught them and adjust the suite, fixtures, or tooling instead of simply adding more shallow tests.
keyPoints: Map tests to risks. Use many fast pure-unit tests for domain logic, focused component tests for rendering and interaction, contract tests for APIs, and a small set of critical end-to-end journeys.
Test behavior through public APIs, not private methods and implementation details. Replace shallow tests that only assert component creation.
Use test harnesses or accessible queries for shared UI components. Avoid arbitrary waits; synchronize on observable outcomes.
Mock at stable boundaries and keep a smaller set of tests against real services or realistic contract fixtures.
Track escaped defects, flakiness, runtime, and mutation score for critical logic rather than celebrating coverage alone.
Run accessibility, visual regression, and performance checks for high-risk components.

blocks.question: The project has thousands of brittle unit tests but still releases defects. How would you redesign the test strategy?
blocks.answer:
I would stop treating test count as the goal. If thousands of tests are brittle and defects still escape, the suite is probably testing implementation details instead of real risk.

First I would map tests to the areas where the product can fail: domain rules, shared UI components, API contracts, permissions, accessibility, and the few journeys that must never break. Pure business logic should have many fast unit tests. Rendering and interaction should be covered by focused component tests.

For Angular components, I would test behavior through the public surface. I prefer test harnesses or accessible queries over private methods and CSS internals. Tests that only assert that a component was created are usually noise unless the setup itself is valuable.

At the boundaries, I would use contract tests and realistic fixtures so frontend and backend changes do not surprise each other. End-to-end tests should be smaller in number, but they should cover critical paths like login, payment, submission, and recovery from errors.

I would also measure the test system. Flakiness, runtime, escaped defects, mutation score for critical logic, accessibility failures, and visual regressions tell me more than raw coverage. The goal is confidence, not a big green number.

title: Testing RxJS and signals
description: Senior/lead scenario: A component combines debounced search, cancellation, a signal view model, and error recovery. How would you test it?

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
RxJS and signals are easiest to test when time, state, and rendering are separated. Time-based streams need controlled time. State transformations need pure tests. Angular rendering needs a small number of component tests that look at behavior.

Cancellation is a key idea here. With search, correctness is not just whether one request succeeds; it is whether old work is ignored when newer user intent arrives.

Signals should not push tests toward private implementation details. Treat them as part of the component's reactive model, then verify the public result through inputs, events, and DOM updates.
keyPoints: Extract pure mapping and state-transition logic where possible and test it without Angular TestBed.
Use virtual time or controlled schedulers for debounce and retry logic so tests are deterministic and fast.
Provide a fake API that lets the test resolve requests in any order to verify cancellation and stale-response protection.
Assert observable user behavior: loading state, latest results, error message, and retry recovery.
For signals, update inputs and flush the framework rendering mechanism rather than reading private implementation details.
Include a destruction test to confirm no late update occurs after the component is removed.

blocks.question: A component combines debounced search, cancellation, a signal view model, and error recovery. How would you test it?
blocks.answer:
I would split the problem before writing tests. The pure parts, like mapping API responses into a view model or deciding state transitions, should be tested without Angular TestBed. That keeps most tests fast and easy to read.

For the RxJS timing, I would avoid real timers. Debounce, retry, and cancellation should use virtual time or a controlled scheduler so the test is deterministic and does not wait in real time.

The fake API needs to let me resolve requests in any order. That is how I prove an older search result cannot overwrite the newest one. I would test loading state, latest results, error message, retry behavior, and the empty state as user-visible outcomes.

For signals, I would interact through inputs, outputs, and rendered DOM instead of reading private fields. After changing an input or signal source, I would flush Angular rendering and assert what the user sees.

I would include teardown behavior too. If the component is destroyed while a request is still pending, a late response should not update the UI or throw an error.

blocks.question: How would you test that a cancelled HTTP request cannot overwrite the newest results?

If the implementation uses `switchMap`, abort signals, or request IDs correctly, the stale response cannot win.

title: Contract testing with backend teams
description: Senior/lead scenario: Frontend and backend teams release independently and frequently break each other with response changes. What process would you introduce?

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
Contract testing is about turning assumptions between teams into executable checks. Frontend and backend can release independently only if each side knows what changes are safe.

The contract should describe the behavior the consumer depends on: fields, allowed nulls, enum expansion, error envelopes, pagination, and deprecation periods. Generated DTOs are useful, but they are not enough by themselves because production JSON can still be wrong.

A good process has checks on both sides. The consumer proves what it needs, and the provider proves it still supplies it.
keyPoints: Publish an explicit API contract using OpenAPI, schema definitions, or consumer-driven contracts. Version behavior, not only URL paths.
Generate or validate DTO types, but also perform runtime validation for untrusted responses at critical boundaries.
Add provider verification in backend CI and consumer contract tests in frontend CI.
Define compatibility rules for optional fields, enum expansion, nullability, pagination, error envelopes, and deprecation periods.
Use representative fixtures and a shared test environment only as an additional check, not as the sole contract.
Make contract ownership and change communication visible.

blocks.question: Frontend and backend teams release independently and frequently break each other with response changes. What process would you introduce?
blocks.answer:
I would make the API contract explicit and part of both teams' CI. TypeScript types in the frontend help developers, but they do not prove the backend is still returning the shape the browser receives at runtime.

The contract could be OpenAPI, JSON schema, or consumer-driven contracts, depending on how the teams work. The important part is that behavior is versioned, not just the URL. Pagination, nullability, optional fields, enum values, errors, and deprecation rules all need to be clear.

In frontend CI, I would test consumers against generated or validated fixtures. In backend CI, the provider should verify that its real responses still satisfy the contract used by the frontend. That catches breaking changes before either side ships.

I would still keep runtime validation at important boundaries. A browser receives untrusted data, and a bad response should fail safely with a clear error path rather than corrupting state or showing misleading information.

Finally, I would make ownership visible. Contract changes need review, communication, compatibility windows, and examples so independent releases do not become accidental breaking changes.

If the backend returns `null`, renames a field, changes an enum value, or sends a different error envelope, the browser will still receive that JSON. Without runtime validation or contract verification, the app may compile cleanly and fail only in production.

title: Legacy AngularJS migration
description: Senior/lead scenario: A profitable application still uses AngularJS and cannot be rewritten in one year. How would you modernize it?

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
Legacy migration is mainly risk management. The code is old, but it is also running a real business, so the plan should reduce risk while creating space for modern development.

A strangler approach works because it changes ownership boundaries gradually. New Angular routes can grow around stable contracts while AngularJS shrinks. The bridge is useful only if it helps the migration move faster and has a clear end.

The key is to migrate valuable slices, not just technology for its own sake. Tests, telemetry, and decommission metrics keep the work honest.
keyPoints: Create a strangler plan around business slices. Freeze new AngularJS patterns and route new features to modern Angular boundaries.
Stabilize shared contracts for authentication, navigation, events, and data. Avoid deep two-way state sharing between frameworks.
