Add characterization tests and production telemetry before changing critical legacy behavior.
Remove obsolete dependencies, tighten CSP, and upgrade build tooling independently where feasible.
Measure migrated traffic, defect rate, bundle/runtime cost, and remaining risk; communicate a funded decommission roadmap.

blocks.question: A profitable application still uses AngularJS and cannot be rewritten in one year. How would you modernize it?
blocks.answer:
I would not plan a big-bang rewrite for a profitable AngularJS app unless there is a very strong reason. The safer path is usually a strangler migration around business slices, where new work moves to modern Angular and old routes are retired over time.

First I would freeze new AngularJS patterns. New features should land behind modern Angular boundaries where possible, with clear contracts for authentication, navigation, events, and data. The two frameworks should not share deep mutable state.

If an upgrade bridge is needed, I would treat it as temporary infrastructure. It should have owners, metrics, and a removal plan. I would rather migrate whole routes or vertical workflows than random leaf components, because users experience workflows, not component inventories.

Before changing critical legacy behavior, I would add characterization tests and production telemetry. The team needs to know what the old system actually does, including edge cases that may not be documented.

In parallel, I would reduce risk by removing obsolete dependencies, tightening CSP where possible, and modernizing build tooling in steps. Progress should be measured by migrated traffic, defects, runtime cost, and the remaining decommission plan.

title: Design-system architecture
description: Senior/lead scenario: Several teams have built different buttons, forms, tables, and accessibility behavior. How would you establish a design system?

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
A design system is shared product infrastructure. It combines visual language, reusable Angular behavior, accessibility, documentation, release management, and governance.

The useful mental model is layers. Tokens define visual decisions. Primitives define behavior and accessibility. Product patterns combine primitives into common flows. Governance decides how teams request, extend, and retire pieces.

Without that structure, a design system becomes either a screenshot library nobody can implement or a bottlenecked Angular package nobody wants to use.
keyPoints: Start with design tokens and foundational primitives, then build high-value components with documented states, accessibility, and content guidance.
Separate visual tokens from component behavior. Support themes through CSS custom properties or generated token artifacts.
Publish components as versioned libraries with semantic versioning, changelogs, migration schematics, and a deprecation window.
Provide examples, do/don’t guidance, design files, test harnesses, and an issue/contribution process.
Measure adoption, duplicate component reduction, accessibility defects, and upgrade cost.
Create governance that enables contribution rather than turning the central team into a bottleneck.

blocks.question: Several teams have built different buttons, forms, tables, and accessibility behavior. How would you establish a design system?
blocks.answer:
I would start with the foundations, not by forcing every team to adopt a giant component library overnight. The first pieces are design tokens, accessibility rules, content guidance, and a small set of high-value primitives like buttons, inputs, dialogs, and tables.

Tokens and component behavior should be separate. Colors, spacing, typography, and themes can be delivered through CSS custom properties or generated token artifacts, while Angular components own interaction, validation display, keyboard behavior, and accessibility.

The design system should be a versioned product. I would publish Angular libraries with semantic versioning, changelogs, examples, test harnesses, migration guides, and deprecation windows. Teams need a clear path to upgrade, not surprise breaking changes.

Governance matters as much as code. Product teams need a contribution process, design files, do-and-don't examples, and a way to request variants without waiting forever on a central team.

I would measure adoption, duplicate component reduction, accessibility defects, upgrade cost, and support load. That shows whether the system is actually helping teams ship consistent experiences.

title: Circular dependency diagnosis
description: Senior/lead scenario: The build succeeds in development but fails intermittently in production because of circular imports. How do you resolve them?

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
A circular import is usually a design smell, not just a TypeScript annoyance. It means the direction of knowledge between modules is unclear.

The right question is: which layer should own this concept? Feature modules should not casually import each other, and utilities should not depend on application features. When the ownership is clear, the dependency direction usually becomes clear too.

Barrels can make this harder because they hide the real path. Tooling and boundaries help keep the architecture understandable as the app grows.
keyPoints: Use dependency graph tooling to identify the cycle and the exact import path, including barrel files that hide it.
Find the ownership error: often two features depend on each other or a low-level utility imports a higher-level feature.
Extract a stable contract, shared model, or orchestration layer only when it represents a real common concept. Do not create a misc folder merely to break the cycle.
Replace direct imports with dependency inversion or events when one domain should not know the other implementation.
Avoid side-effectful module initialization that makes cycle order observable.
Add automated rules so the cycle cannot return.

blocks.question: The build succeeds in development but fails intermittently in production because of circular imports. How do you resolve them?
blocks.answer:
I would start by making the cycle visible. Dependency graph tooling can show the exact import path, including barrel `index.ts` files that hide what is really being imported.

Then I would look for the ownership problem. Circular dependencies often mean two features know too much about each other, or a low-level utility has started importing a higher-level feature. The fix should match the domain issue, not just silence the build.

If there is a real shared concept, I would extract a stable model, contract, or small orchestration layer. If one feature only needs to notify another, an event or dependency-inversion boundary may be cleaner than a direct import.

I would avoid creating a random `shared` or `misc` folder just to break the cycle. That usually moves the mess instead of improving the architecture.

Finally, I would remove side-effectful module initialization where import order matters, then add lint or dependency-boundary rules so the same cycle cannot come back.

title: Angular library versioning
description: Senior/lead scenario: A shared Angular library is used by 25 applications on different release schedules. How do you evolve it safely?

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
Shared library versioning is about protecting consumers on different schedules. The library team owns compatibility, communication, and migration paths, not only package publishing.

A small public API is easier to support because every exported type becomes a promise. Peer dependency rules matter because Angular libraries live inside applications that already bring the framework.

Safe evolution comes from version policy, consumer testing, deprecation windows, and clear release operations.
keyPoints: Publish a clear compatibility matrix for Angular, TypeScript, and peer dependencies. Avoid bundling a second copy of framework packages.
Use semantic versioning based on consumer-visible behavior. Mark deprecations before removal and provide migration examples or schematics.
Test the library against representative consumer applications, not only its isolated unit tests.
Keep public APIs small and avoid exposing internal third-party types unnecessarily.
Automate release notes, provenance, vulnerability scans, and rollback of a bad version.
Track adoption and support parallel major versions only for a defined period.

blocks.question: A shared Angular library is used by 25 applications on different release schedules. How do you evolve it safely?
blocks.answer:
I would treat the shared Angular library like a product with many customers. The first thing I want is a clear compatibility matrix for Angular, TypeScript, RxJS, and peer dependencies so each application knows which versions are safe.

Framework packages should be peer dependencies, not bundled copies. Shipping another Angular or RxJS instance through a library can create hard-to-debug runtime and injection problems.

For changes, I would use semantic versioning based on consumer-visible behavior. Deprecations should come before removals, with examples, migration notes, and schematics when the change is common enough to automate.

The library should be tested against representative consuming apps, not only its own unit tests. A component can pass in isolation and still fail because of build settings, Angular versions, styling assumptions, or dependency conflicts in a real app.

I would keep the public API small and automate release notes, provenance, vulnerability scanning, and rollback. Adoption should be tracked, and parallel major versions should have a defined support window.

title: Third-party widget integration
description: Senior/lead scenario: A chart library mutates DOM directly, leaks listeners, and does not understand Angular signals. How would you integrate it?

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
A third-party widget should be treated as an unsafe boundary. Angular owns data flow and lifecycle; the widget owns its internal DOM. The wrapper translates between those worlds.

The main ideas are containment, lifecycle control, and explicit updates. Without a wrapper, library details leak everywhere and cleanup bugs become hard to find.

Signals do not remove the need for integration discipline. They can drive the wrapper input model, but the wrapper still decides how to update, throttle, sanitize, and destroy the external object.
keyPoints: Wrap it in one Angular component or directive so the rest of the application sees a typed, stable API.
Initialize only after the host element is available, update the instance with minimal diffs, and destroy it deterministically.
Run high-frequency library callbacks outside Angular when they do not update Angular state; re-enter through explicit signal or event updates when needed.
Sanitize or validate HTML labels and URLs accepted by the library. Review CSP compatibility and dependency vulnerabilities.
Lazy load the library if it is heavy and used on limited routes.
Add visual, accessibility, performance, and memory regression tests around the wrapper.

blocks.question: A chart library mutates DOM directly, leaks listeners, and does not understand Angular signals. How would you integrate it?
blocks.answer:
I would isolate the chart library behind one Angular wrapper component or directive. The rest of the app should see a typed Angular API, not direct calls into a DOM-mutating library.

The wrapper would initialize the chart only after the host element exists. Updates should be minimal diffs, not full re-creation on every signal change. On destroy, it must remove listeners, timers, observers, and the chart instance deterministically.

For performance, I would run high-frequency callbacks outside Angular when they do not need to update Angular state. If a callback does need to update the app, I would re-enter Angular through an explicit signal update or output event.

Security still matters. Any HTML labels, URLs, tooltips, or plugin content accepted by the library need validation or sanitization. I would also check CSP support, dependency health, licenses, and known vulnerabilities.

If the library is heavy and used only on a few routes, I would lazy load it. Around the wrapper, I would add visual, accessibility, performance, and memory regression tests because that boundary is where the risk lives.

title: Worker-based computation
description: Senior/lead scenario: Filtering and aggregating 200,000 locally cached rows blocks the UI for two seconds. How would you use a Web Worker?

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
A Web Worker moves CPU work off the main thread, but it does not make work free. It changes where the cost happens and adds communication overhead.

The best worker tasks are pure, chunky computations with small or transferable inputs and outputs. DOM work, Angular rendering, and user interaction still belong on the main thread.

Correctness also needs request identity. If the user changes filters quickly, old worker results must not overwrite newer intent.
keyPoints: First confirm the work is CPU-bound and cannot be moved to the backend or reduced by better data design.
Move pure computation to a worker and define a typed message protocol with request ID, operation, parameters, result, progress, and error.
Avoid repeatedly cloning huge objects. Use transferable buffers or compact columnar data when practical.
Cancel or supersede stale jobs, and ignore late responses by request ID.
Keep DOM access and Angular rendering on the main thread. Return only the data needed for the current viewport.
Measure transfer cost, worker startup, total latency, and memory; a worker is not free.

blocks.question: Filtering and aggregating 200,000 locally cached rows blocks the UI for two seconds. How would you use a Web Worker?
blocks.answer:
I would first confirm that the work really belongs in the browser. If the backend can filter or aggregate the data, or if the UI only needs a smaller dataset, that is usually better than pushing more computation into the client.

If the work is truly CPU-bound and must use locally cached rows, I would move the pure computation into a Web Worker. The worker should have a typed message protocol with a request ID, operation name, parameters, progress, result, and error shape.

I would be careful with data transfer. Sending 200,000 large objects back and forth can cost more than the calculation. When practical, I would use compact data, transferable buffers, or column-style structures instead of cloning huge object graphs repeatedly.

The Angular side should keep DOM and rendering on the main thread. It should send jobs, show progress, cancel or supersede stale jobs, and ignore late responses by request ID.

Finally, I would measure the full path: worker startup, transfer time, compute time, memory growth, and time until the current viewport updates. A worker is useful only if the user experience improves overall.

title: Application startup optimization
description: Senior/lead scenario: The application shows a blank screen for several seconds before the first route. What do you inspect?

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
Startup performance is a chain of costs. The browser must download, parse, execute, bootstrap, fetch required data, and render something useful. Improving it starts by finding which link is slow.

Angular gives several levers: route lazy loading, smaller bundles, careful initializers, SSR or app shells, deferred optional features, and less eager dependency creation. The right lever depends on the trace.

A good answer also distinguishes a pretty loader from a faster app. The goal is a first usable experience, measured on real user devices.
keyPoints: Separate network download, parse/compile, application bootstrap, authentication, configuration, and first API time in the performance trace.
Reduce initial JavaScript and polyfills, remove synchronous startup work, and lazy load non-essential services and routes.
Fetch critical configuration efficiently and cache immutable configuration with versioning. Avoid serial app initializers when work can run in parallel.
Render a stable app shell or server-rendered content rather than a blank page. Keep the loader accessible and honest.
Delay analytics, chat, feature tours, and other third-party code until after the first task is usable.
Set startup budgets by device/network class and monitor real users, not only developer laptops.

blocks.question: The application shows a blank screen for several seconds before the first route. What do you inspect?
blocks.answer:
I would start with a performance trace instead of guessing. A blank screen can come from network download, JavaScript parse and compile, Angular bootstrap, authentication, configuration loading, route resolution, or the first API call.

Once the trace is split, I would reduce the initial work. That means smaller initial JavaScript, fewer polyfills, lazy-loaded routes, no heavy services created at startup, and no synchronous work that blocks the first usable screen.

Configuration and authentication need special attention. Critical config should be fetched efficiently, cached with versioning where possible, and loaded in parallel when it is safe. Serial `APP_INITIALIZER` work can quietly turn startup into a waterfall.

The user should not stare at a blank page. I would render a stable shell, skeleton, or server-rendered content where it fits, with an accessible loader that communicates real loading states.

Third-party scripts like analytics, chat, and product tours should wait until the first important task is usable. Finally, I would set budgets by real device and network class and monitor real users, not only fast developer machines.

title: Multi-tab state synchronization
description: Senior/lead scenario: A user logs out in one tab but other tabs remain active. How would you synchronize authentication and selected application state?

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
Multi-tab sync is distributed state in a small form. Each tab has its own memory, timing, and lifecycle, so the design should use explicit events and clear authority.

The browser channel is for coordination, not for sharing secrets. Tabs should broadcast that something happened, then each tab should update or clear its own state safely.

The tricky parts are stale messages, loops, sleeping tabs, and races. Versioned events and server-side authority keep those cases manageable.
keyPoints: Use BroadcastChannel where supported or a storage event fallback to publish explicit events such as logout, token-state change, or tenant switch.

blocks.question: A user logs out in one tab but other tabs remain active. How would you synchronize authentication and selected application state?
blocks.answer:
I would synchronize only the state that must be shared across tabs. Authentication changes, logout, token state, and tenant switches usually need cross-tab coordination. Local view state, like an open panel or unsaved filter, should usually stay per tab.

For communication, I would use `BroadcastChannel` where supported, with a storage-event fallback if needed. The message should describe intent, such as `logout` or `tenantChanged`, not contain sensitive token values.

Each event should include a version, source tab ID, timestamp, and maybe a sequence number. That helps prevent loops, ignore stale events, and handle older tabs that wake up after being suspended.

Logout must be authoritative on the server. When one tab logs out, other tabs should clear local auth state and stop work, but session revocation on the backend is what actually protects the account.

I would also handle races between refresh and logout. Then I would test tab restore, mobile suspended tabs, browser crashes, and multiple tabs refreshing at the same time.

title: Angular build and bundle governance
description: Senior/lead scenario: Bundle size grows every sprint and nobody owns it. What governance would you establish?

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
Bundle governance is performance management at the code-review and release level. If nobody owns it, every sprint adds a little weight until startup and route changes suffer.

The useful model is user cost, not package vanity metrics. Download, parse, compile, execute, and cache behavior all affect real users differently.

Good governance combines budgets, dependency review, analysis artifacts, lazy-loading checks, and team visibility so performance stays part of normal delivery.
keyPoints: Set initial and route-level size budgets based on user impact. Fail CI on meaningful regression, with an explicit reviewed exception process.
Generate bundle analysis artifacts for pull requests that add significant weight and identify duplicate packages or side-effectful modules.

Track compressed and parsed/executed cost, not only raw package size.
Lazy load heavy optional features and verify that preloading does not negate the split.
Publish a recurring performance scorecard by team or domain without turning it into a blame metric.

blocks.question: Bundle size grows every sprint and nobody owns it. What governance would you establish?

I would make bundle size an owned quality gate, not an occasional cleanup task. The first step is setting initial and route-level budgets based on user impact, then failing CI on meaningful regressions with a reviewed exception process.

Pull requests that add noticeable weight should produce bundle analysis artifacts. Reviewers should be able to see duplicate packages, heavy transitive dependencies, side-effectful modules, and whether tree shaking is working.

Heavy optional features should be lazy loaded, and preloading should be checked so it does not erase the split. I would publish a recurring scorecard by team or domain, focused on improvement rather than blame.

title: CI/CD and safe deployment
description: Senior/lead scenario: A frontend release introduces a critical defect even though the backend did not change. How would you design safer delivery?

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
Safe frontend delivery is about controlling artifact identity, release exposure, and detection speed. A frontend can break without a backend deploy because JavaScript, cached HTML, flags, dependencies, and client logic are all production systems.

The pipeline should prove the artifact, then promote that exact artifact. Deployment should expose it gradually and measure user impact by version.

Rollback and cache strategy are part of the design. If the browser keeps serving the broken shell or service worker, the rollback may not actually reach users.

blocks.question: A frontend release introduces a critical defect even though the backend did not change. How would you design safer delivery?
blocks.answer:
I would design the frontend release so the same tested artifact is promoted through environments. The build should be immutable and versioned, with environment configuration injected safely instead of rebuilding slightly different assets for each environment.

Before release, CI should cover static analysis, unit and component tests, API contract tests, security scans, accessibility checks, and the critical end-to-end journeys. The goal is not to test everything through the browser, but to catch the failures each layer is best at finding.

For production, I would use canary or progressive rollout. Frontend errors, journey success, Core Web Vitals, and API compatibility should be monitored by application version so a bad release is visible quickly.

Risky behavior changes should be behind feature flags, and the frontend should remain compatible with current and previous API behavior during rollout. Backend stability does not guarantee frontend safety if cached assets, flags, or client-only logic changed.

Rollback needs to be real. Static assets, config, and service-worker caches must not keep a broken version alive. After an incident, I would run a blameless review and turn the findings into automated checks.

title: Production incident leadership
description: Senior/lead scenario: A UI defect displays incorrect financial totals for some users. As frontend lead, what do you do in the first hour?

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
Incident leadership is not the same as debugging fast. The lead has to reduce user harm, organize work, protect evidence, communicate clearly, and guide the team toward a safe fix.

Financial display bugs are high risk because the UI may influence user decisions even when backend data is correct. That means severity depends on user impact, transaction impact, and regulatory or support obligations.

Good frontend incident work relies on versioned telemetry, reproducible data, feature flags, rollback paths, and a post-incident loop that improves detection and prevention.
keyPoints: Establish severity, affected users, data integrity, and whether the error is display-only or has influenced submitted transactions.
Stop further harm using a feature flag, rollback, or temporary disablement. Preserve evidence before changing too much.
Create one incident channel, assign roles, communicate verified facts, and correlate client version, API responses, locale, and user journey.
Coordinate with backend, product, operations, risk, and support. Do not speculate in customer-facing communication.
After mitigation, reproduce, fix, validate with representative data, and monitor recovery.
Run a post-mortem covering detection gap, technical cause, process cause, and preventive actions with owners and dates.

blocks.question: A UI defect displays incorrect financial totals for some users. As frontend lead, what do you do in the first hour?
blocks.answer:
In the first hour, I would focus on stopping harm and getting verified facts. For incorrect financial totals, I need to know severity, affected users, whether it is display-only, and whether any submitted transactions used the wrong value.

If users can still be harmed, I would use the fastest safe mitigation: disable the feature, roll back, turn off a flag, or hide the affected action. At the same time, I would preserve evidence such as app version, API responses, feature flags, locale, and screenshots before changing too much.

I would create one incident channel and assign roles. Someone leads, someone investigates, someone communicates, and someone watches metrics. Communication should use verified facts only, especially for customer-facing or risk-facing updates.

The diagnosis should correlate frontend version, route, locale, formatting logic, API payloads, cached data, and user journey. Incorrect totals can come from rounding, timezone, currency, stale state, a bad selector, or a backend response interpreted incorrectly.

After mitigation, I would reproduce the issue with representative data, fix it, validate the fix, and monitor recovery. The post-mortem should cover detection gaps, technical cause, process cause, and concrete preventive actions with owners.

blocks.title: Trade-offs and production validation
blocks.content: Fast mitigation may disable a valuable feature, but leaving incorrect financial totals live is usually worse. Deep diagnosis is important, but it should not delay stopping further harm. I would validate recovery with version-tagged telemetry, representative financial test cases, audit of affected journeys, rollback or flag status, support reports, and post-fix monitoring.
keyPoints: Validate with production builds, Angular/Chrome profiling, network throttling, memory checks, automated tests, accessibility checks, telemetry and rollback rehearsal.

blocks.question: What frontend telemetry would have reduced time to diagnosis?
blocks.answer: I would want telemetry that includes app version, route, feature flag state, locale, currency, user journey step, API correlation ID, and whether totals were calculated on the client or returned by the backend. Performance or error logs should include safe calculation error codes and data-shape validation failures without exposing account values. Those fields would help separate a formatting bug from stale state, bad API data, or a version-specific regression.
blocks.explanation: It is strong because it names the exact frontend context needed to narrow an incorrect-total incident quickly and safely.

title: Architecture decision records
description: Senior/lead scenario: Teams repeatedly revisit decisions such as state management, micro-frontends, and caching. How would you use ADRs?

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
ADRs are organizational memory for architecture. They keep teams from re-litigating the same choices without context, and they explain the trade-offs behind the current system.

The best ADRs are lightweight. They are not essays for every small implementation choice. They document decisions with long life, broad impact, or high reversal cost.

An ADR is also a review mechanism. It should say when the decision might no longer hold, so architecture can evolve without pretending the old choice was always wrong.
keyPoints: Write a short record for decisions with lasting architectural impact. Include context, constraints, options, decision, trade-offs, consequences, and review triggers.
Link evidence such as performance measurements, security requirements, prototypes, and operational cost.
Record rejected options without presenting them as foolish; future constraints may change.
Store ADRs near the code, review them like code, and mark superseded decisions rather than rewriting history.
Do not use ADRs for every small implementation choice. Focus on decisions expensive to reverse or easy to misunderstand.
Review key ADRs during onboarding and architecture changes.

blocks.question: Teams repeatedly revisit decisions such as state management, micro-frontends, and caching. How would you use ADRs?
blocks.answer:
I would use ADRs for decisions that are expensive to reverse or easy for teams to misunderstand. State management, micro-frontends, caching strategy, rendering strategy, and library boundaries are good examples.

Each ADR should be short and useful. I would include the context, constraints, options considered, the decision, trade-offs, consequences, and what would trigger a review later.

Evidence matters. If the decision came from a performance trace, security requirement, prototype, production incident, or operational cost, I would link that evidence so future teams understand why the choice was made.

Rejected options should be recorded fairly. They were not stupid; they may have been wrong for the constraints at the time. Future constraints can change, and the ADR should make that visible.

I would store ADRs near the code, review them like code, and mark old ones as superseded instead of rewriting history. During onboarding or major architecture changes, key ADRs should be part of the conversation.

blocks.explanation: Weak version to avoid: A weak answer is to write long architecture documents after every meeting and never update them. That creates stale paperwork instead of useful decision memory.

blocks.title: Trade-offs and production validation
blocks.content: ADRs improve alignment and onboarding, but too many records can slow teams and bury important decisions. Too few records leave architecture dependent on memory and hallway conversations. I would validate the practice by checking whether ADRs are linked in code reviews, used during onboarding, referenced in later changes, marked superseded when needed, and focused on high-impact decisions.
keyPoints: Validate with production builds, Angular/Chrome profiling, network throttling, memory checks, automated tests, accessibility checks, telemetry and rollback rehearsal.

blocks.question: What would make you reopen a previous architecture decision?
blocks.answer: I would reopen an ADR when its assumptions change. Examples include a new scale requirement, a security constraint, a major Angular capability, repeated incidents, rising operational cost, or evidence that the current decision is blocking teams. I would not reopen it just because someone prefers a different style.
blocks.explanation: It is strong because it uses evidence and changed constraints as the reason to revisit architecture.

title: Mentoring and code review
description: Senior/lead scenario: You lead 12 frontend developers with mixed experience. How do you improve quality without becoming the approval bottleneck?

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
Mentoring through review works best when standards are clear, tools handle routine checks, and feedback teaches judgment. The lead's job is to raise the team's default quality, not personally approve every important line forever.

Automation protects consistency. Human review should spend attention on trade-offs, edge cases, product risk, and maintainability.

Scaling a team also means turning repeated feedback into shared assets. If the same comment appears every week, the system should change, not just the reviewer wording.
keyPoints: Define review standards and automate formatting, linting, tests, dependency checks, and common architecture rules.
Use code owners for high-risk areas, but distribute expertise through pairing, design reviews, and rotating reviewers.
Review correctness, security, accessibility, performance, maintainability, and tests; avoid spending human time on style already enforced by tools.
Explain the reason behind feedback and distinguish blocking issues from suggestions. Praise strong decisions publicly where appropriate.
Track recurring review issues and convert them into examples, guidelines, workshops, or tooling.
Measure lead time and escaped defects so quality controls remain proportionate.

blocks.question: You lead 12 frontend developers with mixed experience. How do you improve quality without becoming the approval bottleneck?
blocks.answer:
I would make quality less dependent on me personally. Formatting, linting, tests, dependency checks, and common architecture rules should be automated so human review can focus on correctness, security, accessibility, performance, and maintainability.

For high-risk areas, I would use code owners, but I would not let expertise stay trapped with one person. Pairing, design reviews, rotating reviewers, and shared examples help more developers learn the standards.

In code review, I would be clear about what blocks a merge and what is a suggestion. When I give feedback, I would explain the reason, not just the rule. That helps people make better decisions next time.

I would also look for patterns in review comments. If the team keeps missing subscription cleanup, accessible labels, state ownership, or API error handling, that should become a guideline, workshop, checklist, lint rule, or reusable helper.

Finally, I would measure whether the process is healthy. Lead time, review wait time, escaped defects, flaky tests, and repeated review issues show whether quality controls are helping or becoming a bottleneck.

blocks.question: How would you handle a senior developer repeatedly ignoring an agreed architecture rule?
blocks.answer: I would handle it privately first and focus on the impact of ignoring the rule, not on status or ego. I would confirm whether the rule is still valid, ask what constraint they are seeing, and agree on a concrete path forward. If they keep bypassing it, I would make it a team and management issue with clear expectations, because seniority includes modeling agreed standards.
blocks.explanation: It is strong because it combines respect, technical review, and accountability without turning architecture rules into personal conflict.

title: Frontend architect trade-off discussion
description: Senior/lead scenario: The product owner asks for delivery in four weeks, while the ideal architecture would take three months. How do you respond?

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
Architecture trade-off discussions are about options under constraints. The architect should translate technical choices into risk, scope, user impact, and future cost.

The strongest approach avoids two traps: saying yes to an unsafe shortcut, or insisting on the ideal architecture without understanding the business need. Good architecture protects essentials while finding the smallest responsible path.

Debt is acceptable when it is intentional, bounded, and repayable. It is dangerous when it hides security, correctness, or operability problems behind delivery pressure.
keyPoints: Clarify the business outcome, deadline rigidity, risk tolerance, expected lifetime, and regulatory constraints before debating technology.
Offer options with explicit scope, cost, risk, and follow-up debt: a safe thin slice, a temporary adapter, or the full platform investment.
Protect non-negotiables such as security, data correctness, accessibility, and operability. Do not label essential engineering as gold plating.
Design the short-term solution with seams for extension and record the debt with owner and trigger for repayment.
Demonstrate trade-offs using evidence and prototypes rather than authority.
After agreement, communicate the decision consistently and own the outcome.

blocks.question: The product owner asks for delivery in four weeks, while the ideal architecture would take three months. How do you respond?
blocks.answer:
I would start by clarifying the business outcome before debating architecture. I need to know how fixed the deadline is, what must be true at launch, how long the solution is expected to live, and whether there are security, accessibility, data correctness, or regulatory constraints.

Then I would present options in plain language. One option might be a safe thin slice that delivers the most important user journey. Another might be a temporary adapter with known debt. A third might be the full platform investment if the product really needs a long-lived foundation.

I would be clear about non-negotiables. Security, correct data, accessibility, monitoring, and rollback are not gold plating. They are part of shipping responsibly.

If we choose a short-term path, I would design seams so the work can grow instead of becoming a dead end. The debt should have an owner, a trigger for repayment, and a visible record, not a vague promise to clean it up later.

I would use evidence where I can: prototypes, performance numbers, incident history, support cost, and examples from the current codebase. Once the decision is made, I would communicate it consistently and own the outcome with the product team.

blocks.title: Trade-offs and production validation
blocks.content: A thin slice can meet the business need quickly, but it may need later rework if demand grows. A full platform reduces future duplication, but it can delay feedback and overbuild for an uncertain product. I would validate the chosen path with explicit acceptance criteria, risk review, production telemetry, rollback rehearsal, debt tracking, and a follow-up trigger based on usage or complexity.
keyPoints: Validate with production builds, Angular/Chrome profiling, network throttling, memory checks, automated tests, accessibility checks, telemetry and rollback rehearsal.

blocks.question: Give an example of technical debt you would accept and one you would refuse.
blocks.answer: I would accept debt like a temporary adapter around an old API if it has tests, a clear owner, and a planned removal trigger. I would refuse debt that risks incorrect financial data, weakens authorization, skips accessibility for a core journey, or ships without monitoring and rollback for a risky change. Shortcuts are negotiable; user safety and operability are not.
blocks.explanation: It is strong because it separates bounded implementation debt from risks that should not be traded away.
